question: With an EU contribution of approximately EUR 400 000, the Erasmus+ Spark project aims to train school leaders, teachers and parents in how to provide comprehensive sexuality education. An approach which, as stated on the project website, involves the ‘whole school community’. Allocating European funds to teach sexual education to children, or to train those who are supposed to pass it on to them, seems quite absurd.

Children have the right to receive a solid education in fundamental skills from their school, whereas regarding sensitive issues such as sexuality, the primary role and responsibility belong to parents. Can the Commission clarify: 1.
What specific content will be developed and disseminated within the framework of the Spark project, which is financed with approximately EUR 400 000 of Erasmus+ funds?

How does it intend to ensure full respect for the right of parents to be involved and to ensure that the education and teaching of their children is in conformity with their own convictions, as enshrined in Article 14(3) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, and whether an explicit informed consent mechanism is planned?

Does it consider it appropriate to continue funding, with EU resources, projects that promote ideologically divisive approaches to sexual education, in an area which the Treaties reserve primarily to the responsibility of the Member States?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) SPARK1 is an ongoing three-year cooperation project between organisations active in the field of school education, led by the Dublin City University and seven partners from Ireland, Cyprus, Greece, Italy and Portugal. It has been selected by the Irish National Agency further to a call for proposals and on the basis of the criteria set out in the call.

SPARK’s main objective is to develop and implement Comprehensive Sexuality Education (CSE) courses across five countries. Using the European approach to micro-credentials, CSE expertise will be exchanged across the partners. The project aims to provide school leaders and teachers with the skill set needed to deliver meaningful CSE lessons, with parental cooperation.

Respect for parental rights under Article 14(3) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union2 is ensured within the distribution of competences established by the EU Treaties. Responsibility for school curricula, teaching arrangements and any consent mechanisms for participation in sexuality education remains with Member States and the competent educational authorities3.

Within the competences of the EU, the Commission contributes to the development of quality and inclusive education by encouraging cooperation between Member States and by supporting and supplementing their action. Beneficiaries of Erasmus+ must ensure full respect for and compliance with the values and rights enshrined in the EU Treaties and in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union.

1 https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/projects/search/details/2024-1-IE01-KA220-SCH-000245697. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/char_2012/oj/eng. 3 According to Article 165 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.
